artifacts.notes: Extent as the retrieving lane measured it: One page image, leaf n28 of the Internet Archive scan of the Missale Romanum, Rome 1570 (editio princeps), carrying Rubricae generales Missalis Tit. I-IV. One leaf only; blackletter. THE RETRIEVING LANE LABELLED THIS ITEM 'Rome 1570 (editio princeps)' AND THAT IS WRONG. The item's own text layer, held unreceipted beside these leaves in the retrieving lane's scratch, prints VENETIIS on the title page and closes, after the register of gatherings, with the colophon 'VENETIIS apud Ioannem Variscum et heredes Bartholomaei Faletti et Socios anno Domini M.D.LXX.' -- the same colophon this edition record already transcribes for its other digitisation. So these bytes are a second scan of the Venice issue, they are filed under that edition rather than under a new one, and the Rome editio princeps that guidance/missals.md section 6 still lists as an outstanding acquisition is NOT held. A record that had taken the lane's label at face value would have asserted a printing history it had not read and would have closed that acquisition item falsely. This artifact is a different digitisation from artifact.catholic-church.missale-romanum.venice-1570.missale-romanum-1570-text-563f4dd2: that one is the Internet Archive item messale-tridentino-di-san-pio-v-1570 and this one is item bub_gb_adC-aRGza70C.
artifacts.rights_basis: The printing reproduced here was published before 1931 and is in the public domain in the United States: the repository's own rights reading, recorded at guidance/missals.md section 5 against Cornell's public-domain chart current at 1 January 2026, is that a work first published abroad before 1931 is in the public domain with no term running. A faithful photographic reproduction of one page of a 1570 printing adds no original authorship of its own. The bytes are retained at 0.70 MB because they are the evidence itself: the book is blackletter, the only optical text layer this library holds for the 1570 Venice issue is of a different digitisation and reads that face badly, and a reader with no network who wants to check a word of this Missal against a page has nothing else here to open.

artifacts.notes:
WHAT THIS IS: uncorrected optical character recognition of a whole 1570 Missal, 84,442 LF-terminated lines, valid UTF-8, no CR bytes, landed as a plain source artifact and nothing more. It is deliberately NOT structured as liturgical records. The prior lt-hist corpus cut the same text into eight markdown 'sections' whose only structural claim was a line range over the downloaded file -- `source_lines: 20001-30324` on its Proprium de Tempore -- so a comparison of two such sections compares the scanner's disagreements rather than the liturgy's, and nothing of that shape is reproduced here. Addressability by identity, this collect of this Mass, belongs to passage records with real loci over these exact bytes, which the schema already supports and which requires reading the pages rather than slicing the file. Until such a passage exists this artifact is a finding aid.

OCR QUALITY, AND IT IS THE WORST OF THE THREE VERSIONS FOLDED IN ON THIS DATE. Measured here by scripts/_ocr_quality.py at a Latin function-word share of 0.0788 over 221,218 tokens, English 0.0211, classified `degraded-latin` -- below the roughly ten per cent at which that tool says running Latin prose sits. The cause is the type: this is a 1570 book set in a blackletter-adjacent face with heavy abbreviation and long s, and the item's own metadata records `ocr_detected_script = Fraktur` at confidence 0.8562 and a Fraktur-trained model. The damage is systematic rather than random. Consonant clusters collapse (`Miffale` for Missale, `celebzande` for celebrandae), Tironian and scribal abbreviations survive as their own codepoints, and whole ornamental initials are emitted as line noise. Individual sentences are nonetheless recoverable: the Ritus servandus reads `cipit Canonem, fecrete oicens To igitur ⁊c.` at line 3083 and `Qui pridie quam pateretur` at line 4173, both plainly the right words badly seen. QUOTE FROM THIS ARTIFACT ONLY THROUGH A CHECKED PASSAGE, AND DO NOT REST A NEGATIVE SEARCH ON IT. At this level of damage a raw-line search establishes neither presence nor absence of a string; it is admitted as indexable so that later passages can pin physical line ranges over it, not so that a search over it can be reported as a finding.

WHAT THE TEXT LAYER CONTAINS AND WHERE, READ RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Quo primum begins at line 84 with its ornamental Q dropped, `Ao primum tempoꝛe ad Zt poftolatue`; the calendar runs from about line 1276 and the computistical matter on the dominical letter from about line 1458; the Ritus servandus runs from about line 2612; the temporal Masses are under way by Holy Thursday at line 28080; and THE CANON IS PRESENT ENTIRE, opening at about line 41209 as `JEi / tiſſime — / — chꝛiſtus / filiumtuum` -- the wreckage of the full-page ornamental T of TE IGITUR, clementissime Pater, per Iesum Christum Filium tuum -- under the running head `canon Miſſe.` at line 41243 and `Canon mile,` at line 41328, with `Hococ eft enim coz: / pue meum` for Hoc est enim Corpus meum at lines 41386 to 41387 and the Nobis quoque list of saints at line 41591.

THE DROPPED INITIALS ARE A SEARCH HAZARD AND ARE NAMED SO THAT NOBODY REPEATS THE MISTAKE MADE WHILE WRITING THIS RECORD. Every large ornamental initial in the book is emitted as line noise or not at all, so the two most quotable openings in a Missal, `Te igitur` and `Quo primum`, are both absent from this text layer as strings while both texts are present in full. A search for either returns only the rubrical references to them in the Ritus servandus. That is the concrete form of the general warning above: an absence here is evidence about the text layer and not about the book.

IDENTITY. The colophon at the end of the file carries a Venice imprint, `VENETIIS / apud Ioannem Variscum, et Heredes / Bartholomaei Faletti, et Socios`, with the year M.D.LXX and a preceding register of gatherings; see the edition record, which refuses the description `editio princeps` on that ground. The item was uploaded on 2021-03-01 by a private uploader crediting `Biblioteca di Alessandria`, in collection booksbylanguage_latin, at 1200 ppi, with no publisher, rights, or creator field beyond an uploader-written description quoting the title. Its identifier and title assert 1570 and the colophon agrees with them.
artifacts.rights_basis: Public domain in the United States because the book was first published outside the United States before the pre-1931 line, and on that ground alone. THE LINE, AND THE YEAR IT WAS DERIVED FOR. Any work first published abroad before 1931 is out of United States copyright; that is the line guidance/missals.md records from Cornell's public-domain chart as current on 1 January 2026, correcting the commissioning brief's 'before 1930'. THE LINE MOVES EVERY JANUARY, which guidance/missals.md:249 states in terms, so it is written here as derived for calendar year 2026 and not as a standing rule: on 1 January 2027 it becomes before 1932, and a later reader must re-derive it rather than quote this sentence. Publication in 1570 clears the line by three hundred and sixty-one years, so no movement of it can ever reach this book and the annual staleness is recorded for the form of the reasoning rather than for any doubt about this row. THE SCAN AND ITS TEXT LAYER ADD NOTHING FOR ANYONE TO OWN. A faithful mechanical reproduction of a public-domain work is not original authorship (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., 36 F. Supp. 2d 191 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)), and machine optical character recognition adds no human authorship on top of it: this text layer was produced autonomously by tesseract 5.0.0-alpha-20201231-7-gc75f run with `-l lat+Fraktur`, per the Internet Archive item's own `ocr` and `ocr_parameters` fields, and there is no author to hold a right in it. NOT RELIED ON, EXPRESSLY: that the Internet Archive item is available, that the download succeeded, or that the host marks it public domain. guidance/sources.md:395-400 holds that availability and successful download are insufficient for `tracked`, and the item's Public Domain Mark 1.0 was the whole of the prior lt-hist corpus's ground for this book -- the ground refused at src/sources/inventories/lt-hist-rights-audit-v1.toml, and the same kind of ground that corpus used to import the 2011 Roman Missal. The mark is recorded as a fact about the item and is not a link in this basis, which would be unchanged if the item carried no mark or a contradictory one.
